description: We are a 6-member multidisciplinary team of systems engineering, data science, and design students working on the astronaut health monitoring challenge for the in-person event at TecNM Zacatepec. Team is currently full.
summary:
Vital-X is a context-aware health monitoring system for astronauts, built as a web app (Ground Control, Crew Display and Wrist) backed by machine-learning research. It knows which mission context each astronaut is in (Earth pre-flight, spacecraft, space station, planetary base, return to Earth, and spacewalks), so it flags real health risks while avoiding false alarms for changes that are expected in that context: 150 bpm is normal during a spacewalk and an alarm at rest.

Deep-space crews face communication delays and link outages, so they must notice problems themselves. Vital-X gives the crew plain-language status and instructions, keeps recording vitals in an onboard "black box" when the link is lost, and delivers everything to Ground Control through Azure Cosmos DB when it returns.

Our Gradient Boosting models, trained on simulated crews calibrated with NASA Human Research Program evidence and tested on unseen astronauts, cut false alarms at launch and reentry from 16.8% (context-blind rules) to 0.0%. All data is simulated; Vital-X supports, and never replaces, flight surgeons.
details:
HOW DOES IT WORK?

1. Mission context. Each astronaut has one task, and the task sets their environment and activity level: Earth pre-flight, spacecraft (launch, transit, reentry), space station, planetary base (Moon/Mars) or return to Earth. Spacewalks (EVA) are tasks done from the station or a base and add suit pressure and suit CO₂.

2. Live monitoring. Vitals update every 3 seconds with a 50-sample history: heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂, temperature, sleep, PVT reaction time, cumulative radiation, hip bone density, vitamin D and left-ventricular mass.

3. Context-adjusted alerts. The app uses limits that change with the environment, activity level and age. An alert is confirmed only after 3 consecutive critical samples, so a single glitch does not alarm. Combined rules (possible suit failure, hypoxia, heat stress, cardiovascular strain) catch several readings drifting together. Each alertcomes with a crew instruction and requires acknowledgement.

4. Three screens. Ground Control for the medical team (whole crew, history, body cam, assignments, environment). ACrew Display tablet with glove-friendly buttons and light-aware themes. A Wrist screen where emergencies take over the display.

5. Offline black box. The astronaut's device records a snapshot every 15 s, with or without a link. During a loss of signal it stores them on the device (IndexedDB) and sends them in order when the link returns. Ground Control reads them from Azure Cosmos DB and shows whether each record arrived live or from the black box, and whether the outage was real or simulated.

6. Risk simulation. For demonstration, Ground can trigger situations based on the events in our training data (dehydration, infection, hypoxia, solar particle event, suit CO₂ failure, suit leak…) or enter readings manually.

7. Machine-learning research. A mission simulator generates crews for ISS, Lunar and Mars missions, calibrated with NASA HRP evidence. Gradient Boosting models detect the mission context from vehicle telemetry (90% accuracy) and the risk level. They use 14-day personal baselines and a 3-day context vote, and are validated with 5-fold cross-validation by astronaut (tested on unseen crew). Results: risk F1 0.71 vs 0.50 for rules, false alarms 1.1% on daily monitoring, 0.0% at launch/reentry (16.8% for context-blind rules), EVA risk F1 0.96 with 0.27% false alarms. In this prototype the web app uses the context-adjusted rules; connecting the models to daily crew reports is thenext step.

BENEFITS

- Fewer false alarms during expected adaptations, so real alerts are trusted (less alarm fatigue).

- Crew autonomy: plain-language status and "what to do now" instructions, without clinical training.

- No data lost during communication blackouts.

- Built for real devices: any sensor or gateway can send to the same API in the same format.

INTENDED IMPACT

As Artemis and future Mars missions move beyond low Earth orbit, real-time telemedicine from Earth becomes impossible. Vital-X is a first line of awareness inside the spacecraft that helps crews act before a health issuebecomes a mission-critical emergency.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Web: React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, Lucide icons, Dexie (IndexedDB), installable PWA (offline-capable),Oxlint.

- Cloud: Vercel (hosting and serverless function) and Microsoft Azure Cosmos DB (telemetry storage).

- Data and ML: Python, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn (HistGradientBoosting, GroupKFold), joblib.

- AI assistants: Claude (Anthropic) and Gemini (Google) for code, documentation and research support under humanreview.

HOW IS IT CREATIVE?

Standard monitors use fixed thresholds that misfire during predictable strain. Vital-X treats physiology as a function of the mission context, explains every alert in plain words, and combines acute vitals (heart rate, SpO₂,suit telemetry) with chronic spaceflight stressors (bone loss, radiation) in one system that keeps working when the link to Earth is lost.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, hostile and closed environments.

- Alarm fatigue and cognitive load: confirmation windows, combined rules, acknowledgement.

- Usability in space: gloves, small wrist screens, lighting conditions.

- Communication delays and outages: store-and-forward black box.

- Ethics and scope: a decision-support prototype; it does not diagnose or treat.

- Data transparency: all data is simulated, and every calibration figure cites its NASA/CSA source.

- Branding: our own identity (Vital-X), no NASA logos or insignia.
